prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, well-defined invention with an unambiguous chain from concept to result: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the motional and light-shift limits of neutral-atom spectroscopy, which allows many atoms to be interrogated at once and fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It has been reproduced and compared across many laboratories, is driving the pending redefinition of the second, and has opened relativistic geodesy and sensitive tests of constants and of dark-sector couplings. All eight members ranked it in their top three, which reflects the fact that the physics, the attribution (Katori for the concept and first realization, Ye for pushing accuracy, stability and many-body regimes) and the maturity all hold up under separate scrutiny. A two-person prize is clean and leaves no obvious injustice within the supplied credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier precision-spectroscopy recognition: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems (including ion-based optical clocks) mean the committee could regard lattice clocks as an incremental extension rather than a new discovery. There is also a timing argument for waiting until the redefinition of the second is formally adopted, and the credit boundary with other lattice-clock contributors (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) and with the Hall and Hansch infrastructure is not fully cleanly drawn by a two-name list.

responses.point: Ranks the CMB acoustic-peak and precision mapping work (B008) first as a mature, field-defining measurement, but concedes that five credited names cannot be cut to three without omitting Planck or Sunyaev.
responses.response: I agree that the CMB program is scientifically central and fully mature, but I do not think the attribution problem you describe can be dismissed: leaving out Planck/HFI and the early theory of acoustic oscillations would be a serious injustice, and the earlier COBE and cosmology prizes narrow what is left to credit. B048 does not have that difficulty, since the supplied pair maps directly onto concept and record-setting realization. I place B008 below B048 for that reason, not because of any doubt about its importance.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B019) first, valuing how a concept translated into material-specific predictions confirmed by experiment, while flagging the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: The materials-prediction argument is persuasive, and I rank B019 as a solid candidate and name it as an alternative. My disagreement is about attribution: the HgTe quantum-well proposal is the step that made the experiment possible, and a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves it uncredited, while the 2016 topology prize narrows the novelty. I would want to see a citation that is explicitly about the Z2 classification and its first observation before placing it above a clock prize whose credit set is more complete.

responses.point: Places circuit QED (B001) first as the architecture of superconducting quantum processors, while acknowledging a possible near-repeat of the 2025 circuit prize and that nearby contributors are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I take the architectural importance seriously, and I recognize you are close to this subject and say so. My concern is the one you raise yourself: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum phenomena in circuits and the uncredited Yale and Devoret/Girvin contributions make both timing and attribution weaker than for the lattice clock. I also see it as partly a platform-engineering success rather than a single decisive discovery, which is why I ranked it only eighth; I would be open to revisiting if the committee judges the 2025 overlap to be minor.

responses.point: Ranks the lattice clock first, noting that she can judge the atomic-structure and systematic-shift physics, and asks whether credit is fairly split between Katori's early proposal and the later precision development.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking, and I think your question about the split is the right one to leave open rather than settle by assertion. My view is that the proposal and first strontium realization (Katori) and the drive to the systematic limit and many-body regime (Ye) are different but equally decisive contributions, and that both belong in the citation. Since you and I both work close to this field, I would welcome your check of the clock-comparison figures, because I am relying on recollection for some priority details and not on verified numbers.

responses.point: Ranks the Higgs experimental discovery (B054) first as foundational and overdue, but admits that any three of the ATLAS/CMS leaders omit deserving people.
responses.response: The scientific case for B054 is overwhelming and I do not dispute its maturity. My objection is to the attribution itself: selecting Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti rather than Della Negra is a choice among thousands of contributors that the statutes force, and it would be hard to defend as a measure of who made the discovery. I would support it as a strong alternative if the committee can agree a citation framed around the detector leadership; I currently rank the clock higher because its credited names reflect personal invention.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 (comb) and 2012 (single-quantum-system control) prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding.
Fair treatment of other lattice-clock contributors outside the credited names, and my reliance on recollection for priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel work.
Whether a second part (for example trapped-ion quantum logic) should share the prize or whether a single achievement is cleaner.
statement.conflict_note: No decisive conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile, but as an experimental atomic physicist who spent time in John Hall's laboratory (Hall is a 2005 laureate whose comb work underlies lattice clocks), I have a field-proximity and a possible indirect scientific link to the precision-spectroscopy community that the committee may wish to note. For B003 and the quantum-memory area (B002) I have a professional proximity through my own work on rare-earth-ion quantum memories, and through Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision; none of those involves the credited people on my preferred configuration.
